justification_text:
Certainly! The point estimates for each of the time horizons—one day, one week, and one month—are driven by a combination of trend analysis, recent movements, and baseline expectations. For example, the one-day forecast likely assumes minimal time for significant new factors to emerge, so I relied on near-term momentum or mean reversion in the underlying data. By the time we move to the one-week and one-month horizons, the influence of longer-term trends, seasonal patterns, or fundamental shifts in the data becomes more relevant.

The width of the confidence intervals reflects the level of uncertainty at each time horizon. On a one-day scale, there is relatively little time for external shocks or unexpected developments to drastically alter the outlook, so the confidence interval is narrow. However, as we extend to one month, the range widens significantly. This broader range accounts for potential changes in underlying conditions, external events, and compounding randomness, all of which tend to increase with time.

Specific risks or events could certainly push outcomes outside the stated intervals, especially at the longer time frames. For example, unexpected macroeconomic developments, major policy announcements, or disruptive geopolitical events could all materially influence the forecast. These risks grow more critical as the time horizon extends, which is why the one-month confidence interval is so much wider. While the forecast incorporates typical uncertainty based on historical patterns, rare or extreme events are inherently difficult to capture with precision, and these could drive outcomes beyond the range we’ve predicted.
